Affenpinscher.summary: A small, wiry-coated toy dog with a monkey-like face, originally bred to hunt rats in German kitchens and stables. It's confident and comical, with a big-dog attitude.
funFacts: "Affenpinscher" is German for "monkey terrier."
The French call it the "diablotin moustachu" — the mustached little devil.
An Affenpinscher named Banana Joe won Best in Show at Westminster in 2013.

Afghan Hound.summary: An ancient sighthound with a long, silky coat, bred to hunt in the mountains of Afghanistan. Aloof and dignified, it's also surprisingly silly with its family.
funFacts: Snuppy, the first cloned dog (South Korea, 2005), was an Afghan Hound.
Pablo Picasso had an Afghan Hound named Kabul who appears in some of his work.
The ring curl at the tip of its tail is a breed hallmark.

Airedale Terrier.summary: The largest of the terriers, the "King of Terriers" was bred in Yorkshire's Aire Valley to hunt otters and rats. It's clever, confident and tireless.
funFacts: Airedales carried messages and stood sentry for soldiers in World War I.
President Warren G. Harding's Airedale, Laddie Boy, reportedly had his own chair at Cabinet meetings.

Akita.summary: A large, powerful spitz breed from the mountains of northern Japan. Akitas are famously loyal and dignified, and reserved with strangers.
funFacts: Hachikō, the Akita who waited for his late owner at a Tokyo train station for nearly ten years, is Japan's symbol of loyalty.
Helen Keller brought the first Akita to the United States in 1937.

Alaskan Malamute.summary: One of the oldest Arctic sled dogs, bred by the Mahlemiut Inuit to haul heavy loads over long distances. Malamutes are strong, friendly and very vocal.
funFacts: It's the official state dog of Alaska.
Malamutes were built for strength and endurance, hauling freight rather than racing.
They're known for "talking" with woo-woo howls instead of barking.

American Bulldog.summary: A muscular, athletic bulldog descended from the working bulldogs of the American South, used on farms to catch livestock and guard property.
funFacts: The breed nearly vanished after World War II and was revived by breeders John D. Johnson and Alan Scott.
Chance, the wisecracking dog in Homeward Bound (1993), was an American Bulldog.

American Eskimo Dog.summary: A fluffy white spitz descended from German spitz dogs brought over by immigrants. Smart and eager to please, "Eskies" were stars of early 1900s circuses.
funFacts: It has nothing to do with the Inuit: it was renamed from "American Spitz" after World War I to avoid anti-German sentiment.
Traveling circuses featured Eskies doing tricks like walking a tightrope.

American Foxhound.summary: A lean, long-legged scent hound developed in colonial Virginia and Maryland for fox hunting. Easygoing at home, it's a tireless runner in the field.
funFacts: George Washington bred foxhounds and is often called a founder of the breed.
It's the state dog of Virginia.

American Hairless Terrier.summary: A small, active terrier descended from the Rat Terrier. Its hairless variety traces back to a single hairless puppy born in Louisiana in 1972.
funFacts: With no coat, it needs sunscreen in summer and a sweater in winter.
It's often suggested for people with dog allergies because it sheds so little.

American Pit Bull Terrier.summary: A muscular, athletic terrier descended from British bull-and-terrier dogs. Recognized by the UKC but not the AKC, it's known for its affection toward people.
funFacts: Pete the Pup, with the ring around his eye in the Our Gang (Little Rascals) comedies, was an American Pit Bull Terrier.
Pit bull–type dogs were popular American family dogs and mascots in the early 1900s.

American Staffordshire Terrier.summary: A stocky, muscular terrier recognized by the AKC in 1936, sharing its roots with the American Pit Bull Terrier. AmStaffs are confident and people-loving.
funFacts: "American" was added to its name in 1972 to tell it apart from the smaller Staffordshire Bull Terrier.
The AKC and UKC registered the same original dogs under different names.

American Water Spaniel.summary: A medium-sized brown spaniel with a curly coat, developed around the Great Lakes to retrieve waterfowl from small boats.
funFacts: It's the state dog of Wisconsin.
Its dense, curly coat sheds water, keeping it warm in cold lakes.

Anatolian Shepherd Dog.summary: A large, rugged livestock guardian from Turkey, bred for thousands of years to protect flocks from wolves. Calm and independent, it makes its own decisions.
funFacts: In Namibia, Anatolians guard livestock from cheetahs, which helps protect the cheetahs from farmers.
It's built to cover huge distances patrolling a flock's territory.

Appenzeller Sennenhund.summary: A medium-sized, tricolor Swiss mountain dog from the Appenzell region, bred to herd cattle and guard farms. It's lively, loud and loyal.
funFacts: It's one of four Swiss Sennenhund breeds, along with the Bernese, Entlebucher and Greater Swiss Mountain Dog.
Its tail curls tightly over its back, unlike the other Swiss mountain dogs.

Australian Cattle Dog.summary: A tough, compact herding dog developed in 19th-century Australia to move cattle over vast distances, partly from Dingo bloodlines.
funFacts: An Australian Cattle Dog named Bluey lived 29 years and 5 months, long the record for the oldest dog.
Puppies are born white; the blue or red speckled coat develops as they grow.
They're also called Blue Heelers or Red Heelers because they nip cattle's heels.

Australian Kelpie.summary: An energetic, intelligent herding dog developed in Australia to work sheep in harsh heat with little supervision.
funFacts: Kelpies are famous for running across the backs of packed sheep to reach the other side of the flock.
The breed is named after a 19th-century dog called Kelpie, itself named for a Scottish water spirit.

Australian Shepherd.summary: A medium-sized herding dog that, despite its name, was developed on ranches in the American West. Aussies are brilliant, energetic and need a job.
funFacts: Its ancestors likely came to America with Basque shepherds who had worked in Australia.
Many Aussies have two different-colored eyes.
The breed became popular through rodeos and horse shows in the 1950s.

Australian Terrier.summary: A small, sturdy terrier developed in Australia to control snakes and rodents and to keep watch over homes and farms.
funFacts: It was the first breed developed in Australia to be recognized and shown there.
The soft topknot of hair on its head is a breed signature.

Basenji.summary: An ancient hunting dog from Central Africa, known as the "barkless dog." Basenjis are curious, independent and remarkably cat-like.
funFacts: Instead of barking, Basenjis make a yodel-like sound called a "baroo."
They groom themselves like cats and have very little doggy odor.
Like wolves, females come into heat only once a year.

Basset Hound.summary: A short-legged French scent hound with long ears and a nose second only to the Bloodhound's. Patient and low-key at home, stubborn on a scent trail.
funFacts: "Basset" comes from the French "bas," meaning low.
Its long ears help sweep scents up toward its nose.
A Basset Hound is the mascot of Hush Puppies shoes.

Beagle.summary: A compact scent hound bred in England to hunt rabbits in packs. Merry and curious, it's one of America's most popular family dogs.
funFacts: Snoopy from Peanuts is a Beagle.
The USDA's "Beagle Brigade" sniffs out banned food and plants at U.S. airports.
A Beagle's nose has around 220 million scent receptors.

Bearded Collie.summary: A shaggy Scottish herding dog with a long coat and a "beard," known for its bouncy, exuberant personality.
funFacts: "Beardies" bounce while herding to see over the flock, and many still bounce when excited.
A Beardie's coat often lightens as a puppy and darkens again as it matures.

Beauceron.summary: A large black-and-tan French herding dog, the "Berger de Beauce," used for centuries to herd and guard sheep.
funFacts: Double dewclaws on the hind legs are a required breed trait.
Beaucerons served as messengers and sentries for the French army in both World Wars.

Bedlington Terrier.summary: A graceful terrier from northern England whose curly coat and arched back make it look like a little lamb.
funFacts: Despite its looks, it was bred by miners to hunt rats and badgers.
It's often described as "a lamb with the heart of a lion."

Belgian Malinois.summary: A short-coated Belgian shepherd that's intense, athletic and highly trainable, now a top choice for police and military work worldwide.
funFacts: A Malinois named Cairo took part in the 2011 raid on Osama bin Laden's compound.
It's named after the Belgian city of Malines (Mechelen).

Belgian Sheepdog.summary: The long-haired, all-black variety of Belgian shepherd, also called the Groenendael, bred to herd and guard sheep.
funFacts: It's named after the village of Groenendael near Brussels, where it was developed.
Belgian Sheepdogs served as messenger and ambulance dogs in World War I.

Belgian Tervuren.summary: The long-coated, fawn-to-mahogany variety of Belgian shepherd, elegant and energetic, named for the village of Tervuren.
funFacts: Its coat darkens with age, often with black tips called an "overlay."
Tervurens excel at agility, obedience and herding trials.

Bernedoodle.summary: A cross between a Bernese Mountain Dog and a Poodle, combining the Bernese's tricolor looks and gentle nature with the Poodle's lower-shedding coat.
funFacts: The first intentional Bernedoodles were bred in 2003 by Sherry Rupke in Ontario, Canada.
They come in tiny, miniature and standard sizes, depending on the Poodle parent.

Bernese Mountain Dog.summary: A large tricolor Swiss farm dog bred to pull carts, drive cattle and watch over farms in the canton of Bern. Gentle and good-natured.
funFacts: It's the only one of the four Swiss mountain dog breeds with a long coat.
Berners pulled carts of milk and cheese to market.

Bichon Frise.summary: A cheerful little white dog with a powder-puff coat, once a favorite of European royalty and later a street and circus performer.
funFacts: Its name is French for "curly lap dog."
Bichons traveled with sailors and were reportedly used as barter on trade voyages.
Their coat sheds very little.

Black Russian Terrier.summary: A large, powerful guard dog created by the Soviet Army's Red Star Kennel in the 1950s. Calm and confident, it's devoted to its family.
funFacts: It isn't a true terrier: about 17 breeds, including the Giant Schnauzer and Rottweiler, went into it.
It was bred to guard military installations.

Black and Tan Coonhound.summary: A big American scent hound bred to trail raccoons at night and "tree" them, baying until the hunter arrives.
funFacts: It was the first coonhound breed recognized by the AKC, in 1945.
Hunters can recognize their own coonhound's bay from far away.

Bloodhound.summary: The scent-tracking champion of the dog world, descended from hounds kept by monks at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert in Belgium.
funFacts: Bloodhound tracking evidence has been accepted in U.S. courts.
Its long ears and loose skin help trap scent around its face.
A Bloodhound named Tigger held the record for the longest dog ears, over 13 inches each.

Bluetick Coonhound.summary: A speckled-blue coonhound from the American South with a big voice and a cold-trailing nose.
funFacts: Its "blue ticked" look comes from black ticking over a white coat.
Smokey, the University of Tennessee's mascot, is a Bluetick Coonhound.

Border Collie.summary: Widely considered the most intelligent dog breed, bred on the border between Scotland and England to herd sheep with an intense stare.
funFacts: A Border Collie named Chaser learned the names of more than 1,000 toys.
They control sheep with an intense stare called "the eye."

Border Terrier.summary: A scrappy working terrier from the Cheviot Hills, small enough to follow foxes underground but leggy enough to keep up with horses.
funFacts: Its head is often described as "otter-like."
Border Terriers ran with foxhounds and bolted foxes from their dens.

Borzoi.summary: A tall, elegant Russian sighthound once kept by the aristocracy to hunt wolves. Calm and quiet indoors, lightning fast outside.
funFacts: "Borzoi" means "swift" in Russian.
The breed used to be called the Russian Wolfhound.

Boston Terrier.summary: A compact, tuxedo-coated companion developed in Boston in the late 1800s from bulldog and terrier crosses.
funFacts: Its black-and-white markings earned it the nickname "the American Gentleman."
It's the state dog of Massachusetts.
It was one of the first American breeds recognized by the AKC, in 1893.

Bouvier des Flandres.summary: A big, rough-coated Belgian farm dog bred to herd cattle, pull carts and guard the farm.
funFacts: Its name means "cow herder of Flanders."
President Ronald Reagan had a Bouvier named Lucky.

Boxer.summary: A muscular, playful German breed descended from mastiff-type hunting dogs, known for its exuberance and patience with children.
funFacts: Boxers often stand on their hind legs and bat with their front paws when they play.
The Boxer was one of the first breeds used as a police dog in Germany.

Boykin Spaniel.summary: A small brown hunting spaniel developed in South Carolina to retrieve turkeys and ducks from small boats.
funFacts: It's the state dog of South Carolina.
The breed traces back to a stray spaniel named Dumpy, found near a church in Spartanburg in the early 1900s.

Briard.summary: An ancient French herding dog with a long, wavy coat, often described as "a heart wrapped in fur."
funFacts: Like the Beauceron, it has double dewclaws on its hind legs.
Briards served with the French army in World War I as sentries and in searching for the wounded.

Brittany.summary: An athletic, leggy bird dog from northwest France that both points and retrieves. Bright, upbeat and full of energy.
funFacts: Many Brittanys are born with a naturally short tail or none at all.
The AKC dropped "Spaniel" from its name in 1982 because it hunts more like a pointer.

Brussels Griffon.summary: A tiny Belgian toy dog with an almost human expression, originally kept by cab drivers to keep rats out of their stables.
funFacts: Verdell, the dog in As Good as It Gets (1997), was a Brussels Griffon.
Its expressive face is often said to have inspired the look of Star Wars' Ewoks.

Bull Terrier.summary: A muscular English terrier famous for its unique egg-shaped head and clownish, mischievous personality.
funFacts: Bullseye, Target's mascot, is a Bull Terrier.
General George S. Patton's Bull Terrier was named Willie.

Bullmastiff.summary: A powerful English guardian created in the 1800s by crossing Mastiffs and Bulldogs to stop poachers on large estates.
funFacts: Gamekeepers called it the "gamekeeper's night dog."
Bullmastiffs were trained to pin poachers down rather than bite them.

Cairn Terrier.summary: A shaggy little working terrier from the Scottish Highlands, bred to hunt foxes and rodents among piles of stones called cairns.
funFacts: Toto in The Wizard of Oz (1939) was played by a Cairn Terrier named Terry.
Cairns love to dig, a leftover from hunting among the rocks.
